title: Garlic green beans
skill: Blanching, the shimmer test, a quick sauté

notes.text: Blanch the beans in two batches so the water stays at a boil, and sauté them in two batches so they blister instead of steaming.

move.title: Blanch, shock, then a hot pan
move.body: Green beans get two kinds of heat today. First a quick boil in salted water, then straight into ice water, which is called blanching and shocking. Then a fast sauté in shimmering oil with garlic, so they blister in spots but stay bright green and snap when you bite.

callback.body: In the stir-fry you heated oil until it shimmered and added the garlic last so it wouldn't burn. A sauté works the same way, just with a little less heat and a little more time. This week you'll learn to read the oil before anything goes in.

why.title: Salt the water
why.body: Beans soak up some of the water they boil in. Salted water seasons them all the way through, which salt sprinkled on at the end can't do.

why.title: Why they turn brighter
why.body: A green bean's skin has tiny pockets of air that make the color look dull. A minute in boiling water drives the air out, and the green shows through bright. Cook them too long, though, and the acids inside the bean turn the green a dull olive.

why.title: Shock to stop the cooking
why.body: Hot beans keep cooking from their own heat after they leave the pot. Ice water cools them in seconds, so they stay crisp and bright instead of going soft on the counter.

why.title: Dry before the oil
why.body: Water and hot oil don't mix. Drops of water make the oil spit, and wet beans steam instead of blistering. Patting them dry keeps the pan hot and the oil calm.

why.title: The shimmer test
why.body: As oil heats, it gets thinner, and its surface starts to ripple like a heat haze. That shimmer means it's hot enough to sauté. If it smokes, it's too hot: slide the pan off the heat for a minute.

why.title: Garlic goes in last
why.body: Minced garlic burns in under a minute in a hot pan and turns bitter. Added at the end on lower heat, for just 30 seconds, it stays sweet and golden.

wrong.sign: The beans are olive green and floppy
wrong.fix: They boiled too long, or sat warm before the ice water. Next time, start the timer the moment they go in, and have the ice water ready first.

wrong.sign: The oil spat when the beans went in
wrong.fix: The beans were still wet. Pat them drier next time, and lay them in the pan away from you.

wrong.sign: The garlic turned brown and bitter
wrong.fix: The pan was too hot, or the garlic was in too long. Turn the heat down before it goes in, and keep it moving for just 30 seconds.

wrong.sign: The beans squeak and taste raw
wrong.fix: They needed a little longer in the boiling water. Next time, taste one at 3 minutes, and give them another minute if it's still hard.

quiz.q: Why do the blanched beans go straight into ice water?
choices: To stop the cooking so they stay crisp and green
To make them easier to cut
quiz.explain: That's shocking. Their own heat would keep cooking them.

quiz.q: How do you know the oil is hot enough to sauté?
Why pat the beans dry before they go in the pan?
choices: Water makes hot oil spit and stops the beans browning
So the garlic sticks to them
quiz.explain: Wet food steams instead of browning.

steps.text: Fill the large pot about three-quarters full of water and add {qty:salt} salt. Put the lid on and bring it to a big, rolling boil over high heat.
steps.tip: Trim the beans and mince the garlic while the water heats.

steps.text: Fill the large bowl halfway with cold water and add two big handfuls of ice. Set it next to the stove with the slotted spoon.
Line up a handful of beans with their stem ends even, and cut the stem ends off together. Do the rest the same way. The thin tail ends can stay.
steps.tip: Use the claw on the bundle, knuckles against the blade.

steps.text: Peel the garlic and mince it fine. Put it in the small bowl next to the stove.
Take the lid off and lower the beans into the boiling water a handful at a time with the slotted spoon. Boil them with the lid off.
steps.look: Bright green and a little bendy, but still with a snap when you bite one.

steps.text: Scoop the beans out with the slotted spoon and put them straight into the ice water. Stir them around, and leave them until they're cold all the way through. Turn off the burner under the pot.
steps.tip: Leave the hot pot on the stove to cool. Don't carry it to the sink.

steps.text: Pour the beans and ice water into the colander in the sink. Pick out any ice, then spread the beans on the kitchen towel and pat them dry.
Heat the oil in the skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers.
steps.look: The oil ripples like a heat haze and runs as thin as water when you tilt the pan, but isn't smoking.

steps.text: Lay the beans in the pan in one layer, away from you. Leave them alone for 1 minute, then toss them with the tongs every 30 seconds until they're hot through and blistered in spots.
steps.look: A few brown blisters, and still bright green.

steps.text: Turn the heat down to medium. Push the beans to the edges, add the garlic to the middle, and stir it for 30 seconds. Then toss it through the beans.
steps.look: It smells strong and is pale gold, not brown.

steps.text: Turn off the stove. Add the beans' salt, the pepper, and the lemon juice, and toss. Taste one, add a pinch more salt if it needs it, and serve right away.

notes.text: Sauté the zucchini in four batches so every piece touches the pan.

move.title: A hot pan and room to brown
move.body: Zucchini is mostly water, so it goes soft and soggy in a crowded or cool pan. Today you'll heat the oil until it shimmers, sauté zucchini in batches with space around each piece so it browns, and add garlic at the end.

add.title: Cook in batches
add.body: Every piece needs to touch the hot pan. Crowd it, and the zucchini lets out water that cools the pan, so it steams and goes soft instead of browning.

add.title: Salt at the end
add.body: Salt pulls water out of zucchini. Salted in the pan, it puddles and steams. Salted at the end, it stays browned and firm.

wrong.sign: The zucchini is pale and soggy
wrong.fix: The pan was crowded or not hot enough. Next time, cook it in batches and wait for the shimmer.

wrong.sign: The garlic turned brown and bitter
wrong.fix: The pan was too hot, or the garlic was in too long. Turn the heat down before it goes in, and keep it moving for just 30 seconds.

wrong.sign: It's browned outside but hard in the middle
wrong.fix: The pieces were too thick. Cut them ½ inch thick, all the same.

quiz.q: Why sauté the zucchini in batches?
choices: A crowded pan steams it instead of browning it
quiz.explain: Each piece needs to touch the hot pan.

quiz.q: How do you know the oil is hot enough to sauté?
Why is the zucchini salted at the end?
choices: Salt pulls out water that would make it soggy
Salt burns in a hot pan
quiz.explain: Salted early, it steams in its own water.

add.text: Cut the ends off the zucchini. Cut each one in half the long way, lay the halves flat side down, and slice them across into half-moons ½ inch thick.
add.look: Half-moons all about the same thickness.
add.tip: Use the claw, knuckles against the blade.

heat.text: Heat 1 tablespoon of the oil in the skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers.
heat.look: The oil ripples like a heat haze and runs as thin as water when you tilt the pan, but isn't smoking.

saute.text: Lay a third of the zucchini in the pan, flat side down, with space between the pieces. Leave it alone until the bottoms are golden, then turn each piece and brown the other side. Move it to the plate. Do the other two batches the same way, with another tablespoon of oil each time.
saute.look: Golden brown on both sides, and just tender when you poke one.

garlic-in.text: Turn the heat down to medium. Add the garlic to the empty pan and stir it for 30 seconds. Put all the zucchini back and toss it with the garlic.
garlic-in.look: It smells strong and is pale gold, not brown.

finish.text: Turn off the stove. Add the salt, the pepper, and the lemon juice, and toss. Taste a piece, add a pinch more salt if it needs it, and serve right away.
